prompt: Which of the three tools does this course install from Ubuntu's own archive with `apt`?
hint: Ubuntu packages one of them in a current version; the other two arrive as zip files.

choices.text: The Kotlin compiler, as the package `kotlin`
choices.why: Ubuntu does not package a current Kotlin, which is why section 02 downloads the zip from the Kotlin project.

choices.text: The JDK, as `openjdk-21-jdk-headless`
choices.why: Right: the JDK comes from `apt`, and Kotlin and Gradle are unpacked into `~/.local/share`.

choices.text: Gradle, as the package `gradle`, pinned to 9.8.2
choices.why: Gradle 9.8.2 comes from `services.gradle.org` as a zip; Ubuntu's own `gradle` package is far older.

choices.text: All three, in one `apt install` line
choices.why: One `apt` line installs the JDK, `unzip` and `curl`; the other two tools are downloaded.

prompt: What does `-headless` in `openjdk-21-jdk-headless` leave out?
hint: Think about what a server, or this course, never does on screen.

choices.text: The compiler, so it runs programs and builds none
choices.why: That is the difference between a `-jre` and a `-jdk` package, not what `-headless` means.

choices.text: The JIT compiler, so programs run interpreted
choices.why: A headless JVM compiles hot code to machine code exactly like the full one.

choices.text: The libraries for drawing windows and graphics
choices.why: Right: nothing in this course draws a window, and Android draws its own.

choices.text: The documentation and the source of the standard library
choices.why: Those are separate packages in Ubuntu (`-doc`, `-source`) and have nothing to do with `-headless`.

prompt: Before downloading, `apt` said how much disk the JDK, `unzip` and `curl` would take. How many megabytes?
hint: The line starts with `After this operation`.

prompt: `sha256sum -c` printed `kotlin-compiler-2.4.21.zip: OK`. What has it established?
hint: It compared two things. Where did each come from?

choices.text: That the zip unpacks without errors
choices.why: It never opens the zip; it hashes the bytes. A matching hash implies the bytes are the published ones, which is a stronger statement.

choices.text: That the bytes on disk are the ones the project published
choices.why: Right: it recomputed the checksum of the file and compared it with the one downloaded beside it.

choices.text: That the compiler inside is compatible with Java 21
choices.why: A checksum says nothing about compatibility; `kotlinc -version` is what found the JVM.

choices.text: That GitHub's certificate was valid for the whole of the download
choices.why: That is `curl`'s job, and it would have refused to download before `sha256sum` ran at all.

prompt: Match each command to what it does in this course.
hint: Section 02 asks each of them what version it is.

pairs.right: Compiles `.kt` files into classes or a jar
Starts a JVM and runs a jar
Builds whole projects, from lesson 14 on
Compiles Java source, which this course does not write

right_distractors: Installs the Android SDK and an emulator

prompt: A terminal answers `bash: line 1: kotlinc: command not found`, and `~/.local/share/kotlinc/bin/kotlinc -version` works. What is the cause?
hint: The full path proves something about the file.

choices.text: The zip was damaged, and `kotlinc` is missing from the unpacked files
choices.why: The full path ran the compiler, so the file is there and works.

choices.text: Java is not installed, so the shell hides `kotlinc`
choices.why: Without Java the script is found and then fails naming `java`, a different message.

choices.text: The terminal read `~/.bashrc` before the line was there
choices.why: Right: the terminal was open before `~/.bashrc` gained its line; `source ~/.bashrc` or a new terminal fixes it.

choices.text: `kotlinc` needs `sudo` to run from a home directory
choices.why: Nothing in this course runs the compiler as root, and the full path worked as ana.

prompt: What exit status does the shell give a command it cannot find?
hint: `echo $?` printed it twice in this lesson.

prompt: `kotlinc -version` prints `/home/ana/.local/share/kotlinc/bin/kotlinc: line 102: java: command not found`. What does that tell you?
hint: Which program does the message name, and who printed it?

choices.text: `kotlinc` was found and ran, and could not start a JVM
choices.why: Right: the compiler is a script around a JVM, and the missing program is `java`. The fix is the JDK.

choices.text: `kotlinc` is missing, and line 102 is where the shell searched
choices.why: The message comes from inside `kotlinc`'s own script, so `kotlinc` was found.

choices.text: The compiler needs Java 17 and found a newer one
choices.why: No Java was found at all; a version mismatch would print a version.

choices.text: `PATH` is missing `~/.local/share/kotlinc/bin`
choices.why: Then `bash` would have said `kotlinc: command not found`, naming `kotlinc`.

prompt: A friend's download of the Gradle zip stopped at 90 MB, and they did not keep any checksum. What is the quickest sign the file is damaged?
hint: Section 03 names two signs that need no checksum.

choices.text: The file name lacks `-bin`
choices.why: A cut download keeps the name it was given; nothing about the name changes.

choices.text: `gradle --version` prints an older version
choices.why: A damaged zip cannot be unpacked, so there is no `gradle` to ask.

choices.text: `ls -l` shows less than the zip's full 145 MB
choices.why: Right: the size is the cheapest check, and `unzip` would then fail on the missing central directory.

choices.text: `unzip` asks for the next disk of a multi-part archive
choices.why: `unzip` mentions multi-part archives as one possible explanation, and asks for nothing; the size says it first.

prompt: Why was `hello.jar` 5.5 MB for a program of three lines?
hint: What did `-include-runtime` put in it?

choices.text: It holds a copy of the JVM, so it runs without Java
choices.why: A jar never carries a JVM; `java -jar` is what runs it.

choices.text: It carries Kotlin's standard library
choices.why: Right: without `-include-runtime` the same program was a jar of about a kilobyte.

choices.text: `kotlinc` writes debugging information for every line of the program
choices.why: Debug information for three lines is a few bytes; the small jar showed how little the program is.

choices.text: The jar is compressed less than a zip
choices.why: A jar is a zip, compressed the same way.

prompt: The functions of `Hello.kt` that sit outside any class are compiled into a class called `___`.
hint: `unzip -l` listed it.

prompt: `courses-small.jar` was compiled without `-include-runtime`. `java -jar` fails with `NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/collections/CollectionsKt`, and `kotlin courses-small.jar` works. Why did `hello`'s small jar run with plain `java` while this one does not?
hint: Where did the body of `println` end up?

choices.text: `println` is part of Java, and `listOf` is part of Kotlin
choices.why: Both are Kotlin functions; `println` is inline, so its body was copied into `HelloKt`.

choices.text: `println` is inline and was copied into the program, while `listOf` lives in the standard library
choices.why: Right: an inline function leaves no call to the library behind, and `listOf` does.

choices.text: The second jar was compiled for a newer JVM than the one installed
choices.why: A version problem fails with `UnsupportedClassVersionError`, and both jars came from the same compiler.

choices.text: `joinToString` needs `kotlin-reflect`
choices.why: The missing class is `CollectionsKt`, part of the standard library, which `kotlin` adds.

prompt: `Typo.kt:3:5: error: unresolved reference 'printn'.` What does `3:5` give?
hint: The first line of the file is the comment naming it.

choices.text: The error code and its severity
choices.why: Kotlin's messages carry no numeric codes; the word `error` is the severity.

choices.text: The line and the column where the unknown name starts
choices.why: Right: line 3, column 5, which is where `printn` begins after four spaces of indentation.

choices.text: Three errors found, five lines checked
choices.why: There was one error, and the numbers are a position in the file.

choices.text: The version of the compiler that refused to build the file
choices.why: The version is what `kotlinc -version` prints; the message gives a place in the file.

prompt: What happens when a program assigns a second value to a `val`?
hint: `Reassign.kt` tried it.

choices.text: The program runs and keeps the first value
choices.why: It never runs: the error is at compile time.

choices.text: It throws an exception when that line runs
choices.why: Kotlin catches this before anything runs, which is the point of `val`.

choices.text: The compiler refuses: `'val' cannot be reassigned`
choices.why: Right, and no jar is written.

choices.text: The compiler warns, and quietly turns the name into a `var`
choices.why: The compiler changes nothing on its own; you would make it a `var` yourself.

prompt: `val sessions = mutableListOf(45, 30)` and then `sessions.add(60)`. What happens?
hint: What does `val` fix: the name, or the object?

choices.text: A compile error, because `sessions` is a `val`
choices.why: `val` forbids pointing the name elsewhere, not changing the list it points at.

choices.text: The list grows to `[45, 30, 60]`
choices.why: Right: the name still points at the same list, which is mutable.

choices.text: A new list is made and `sessions` keeps the old two items
choices.why: `add` changes the list in place and returns a `Boolean`; nothing new is made.

choices.text: An exception at run time, since the list is frozen
choices.why: `mutableListOf` makes a list that can change; a frozen one is a different type, lesson 5.

prompt: Which habit does the section recommend?
hint: The compiler is what makes the habit cheap.

choices.text: `var` for everything, then `val` once the program works
choices.why: That is the habit most programmers arrive with, and it is the reverse of the advice.

choices.text: `val` for numbers and `var` for objects
choices.why: The choice depends on whether the name is pointed elsewhere, not on its type.

choices.text: `val` first, and `var` where the compiler shows a name has to change
choices.why: Right: the few `var`s left then mark the places where something changes.

choices.text: `val` inside functions and `var` at the top of a file
choices.why: Where a name is declared does not decide it.

prompt: Match each value to the type the compiler infers for it.
hint: `Types.kt` printed them.

prompt: `val minutes = 45`. What does `println(minutes / 60)` print?
hint: Two `Int`s divide to an `Int`.

prompt: `val minutes: Int = 45` and then `val total: Long = minutes`. What does the compiler do?
hint: Java would have accepted it.

choices.text: It widens the `Int` to a `Long`, as Java does
choices.why: Kotlin does not widen a number for you, even when the value fits.

choices.text: It refuses until you write `minutes.toLong()`
choices.why: Right: `initializer type mismatch: expected 'Long', actual 'Int'`.

choices.text: It compiles, and fails at run time with a `ClassCastException`
choices.why: The mismatch is caught at compile time; nothing runs.

choices.text: It infers `total` as `Int` and ignores the annotation
choices.why: A declared type is checked, never ignored.

prompt: You write `val total = 0` and later add `Long` values to it in a loop. Why does the section say to write the type here?
hint: What does the literal `0` alone make?

choices.text: Inference does not work for a `var`
choices.why: Inference works for `val` and `var` alike; the trouble is what it infers.

choices.text: A name without a type is checked only at run time
choices.why: Every name has a type at compile time, written or inferred.

choices.text: `0` infers `Int`, and adding a `Long` to an `Int` name does not compile
choices.why: Right: `val total: Long = 0` says what the literal cannot.

choices.text: It makes the program faster
choices.why: A declared and an inferred type compile to the same bytecode.

prompt: `val course = "Kotlin"`. What does `println("$course.length")` print?
hint: Where does a name after `$` end?

choices.why: That needs braces: `${course.length}`.

choices.text: `Kotlin.length`
choices.why: Right: the template takes `course`, and `.length` is ordinary text after it.

choices.text: A compile error, because `.length` is not allowed in a string
choices.why: Any text is allowed; it simply is not part of the template.

choices.text: `$course.length`, since templates need braces
choices.why: A bare name works without braces, so `$course` is replaced.

prompt: A raw string opens and closes with three quotes, and `___()` removes the indentation its lines share.
hint: `Report.kt` called it on the weekly report.

prompt: A line reads `course.uppercase()` on its own, and the next prints `course`. What does it print, if `course` was `"kotlin"`?
hint: What does `uppercase()` do with the original?

choices.text: `kotlin`
choices.why: Right: the call built `KOTLIN` as a new string and nothing kept it.

choices.text: `KOTLIN`
choices.why: A `String` never changes; the result was thrown away.

choices.text: `Kotlin`
choices.why: That is `replaceFirstChar`, and its result would also need keeping.

choices.text: A compile error, as `course` is a `val`
choices.why: `uppercase()` does not reassign `course`, so the `val` is not involved.

prompt: In Kotlin, what does `a == b` compare when both are strings?
hint: It is not the Java habit.

choices.text: Whether `a` and `b` are the same object in memory
choices.why: That is `===` in Kotlin, and `==` in Java.

choices.text: Their characters, by calling `equals`
choices.why: Right: Kotlin's `==` calls `equals` for you.

choices.text: Their lengths, then their first characters
choices.why: Equality compares all the characters, not a summary.

choices.text: Their characters ignoring case
choices.why: That needs `equals(b, ignoreCase = true)`.

prompt: Which of these programs fail to compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the lesson's refusals are here, in new clothes.

choices.text: `val week = 44` then `week = 45`
choices.why: Yes: a `val` cannot be reassigned.

choices.text: `val list = mutableListOf(1)` then `list.add(2)`
choices.why: No: the list changes, the name does not.

choices.text: `val hours: Double = 2`
choices.why: Yes: `2` is an `Int`, and Kotlin does not widen it; `2.0` compiles.

choices.text: `var total = 0L` then `total += 45`
choices.why: No: `0L` is a `Long`, and an `Int` literal added to a `Long` gives a `Long`.

prompt: `val minutes = 135`. What does `"${minutes % 60}"` produce?
hint: `%` is the remainder of whole-number division.
